AW-STUDY-0062

The Scene Builder Lab

Status: drafted · concept study and clickable mock, not in the game

A place inside Abbie's World where you choose an asset family, a season, a land shape and how alive it should be, watch the game decorate a first pass, then take over and build freely. Behind a flask button sits a real engineering bench for weather, physics and topology, so the lab can grow into a serious tool without ever greeting a six-year-old with a wall of sliders.

The mock on the Lab tab is playable: everything you see is driven by a small scene document, so undo, "rebuild from record" and the scene file you can copy are real. The pictures are stand-in shapes; the real build draws the model library.

1. What Evan asked for, in one list

  • A scene editor where you mix and match elements and the game generates the world dynamically, with free build on top.
  • A right panel with all the tools and an overlay toolbar.
  • A major build, a first-class in-game engineering lab; not a proof of concept.
  • Experiments with weather, physics, topology, simulation parameters like gravity, without overwhelming anyone.
  • The default path: pick asset family, season, topology, simulation style; first pass auto; second pass the user.

2. The default experience: four choices, then your hands

The three dots at the top left of the lab show where you are. Changing a choice after you have started never throws your work away: the first pass is re-run around the things you placed or pinned. Build my world and the dice card re-roll only the part the game made.

Why this order

Townscaper has one palette and nothing else; Tiny Glade has a tools tray; both let the machine do the tedious detail so the child does the choosing. The first pass is the machine's half of that deal. The second pass is what makes it the child's world, and every edit we let them make is recorded so the machine can keep learning what they like.

Card tray (bottom, hex cards)The family's things as 3D hex cards with counts; the dice card re-rolls the first passMatches the UI layout canon (bottom = real 3D hex cards) and the Minecraft hotbar habit: keys 1 to 9.

Stepper (top left)Choose · First pass · YoursTells a new player where they are without a tutorial.
Play mode (screen icon, or P)Everything folds away, one close button remainsThe cover test: the lab shows its own interface percentage bottom left (about a third of a laptop screen with everything open, because it is a workbench); Play mode drops it to under 1%.
Two layers that never mix. The hex glow, hover ring, selection ring, brush ghost and every panel are presentation layer: characters, creatures and the AI directors cannot see them. Only things you placed exist in the world. There are no axes, gizmos or debug boxes; the grid is glowing hex lines, which the town already uses, and raw numbers show only in developer mode.
Where this sits among the four ways of acting. The lab is "tiles create the world" at full strength, plus a workbench for the grown-up. It is not the god cards (those stay for play: weather and events as cards on the board) and it is not FPS (Step in only lends you eye height to check your work). The lab's right panel is allowed because it is a mode you enter and leave; the play HUD stays at 8% with zero words.

4. Never overwhelming: the disclosure ladder

  • Nothing from a deeper level appears unless asked. The flask pulses gently on the rail; that is its only invitation.
  • Every bench value has a plain-language preset first (Earth, Mars, Moon, Jupiter before the gravity number), a unit, a range and a reset.
  • Defaults come from the four choices. Picking the Moon family nudges gravity to lunar unless you set it yourself. The helper explains any change it makes.
  • Values belong to the scene, not the device, so a world shared with a friend behaves the same.

5. How it is built: a scene is a recipe, not a picture

This is the part that makes the lab a first-class tool and not a toy. Following the modeler vision (preserve creative intent so whole experiences can be rebuilt and upgraded), a scene is saved as a base recipe plus an ordered list of edits, never as a pile of meshes. The mock does exactly this: undo is "drop the last edit and replay", "Rebuild from record" proves the replay gives the same checksum, and the Scene tab shows the record.

Rules the document keeps

  • Determinism. The same recipe and ops give the same world (the mock checks this with a checksum). That is what makes undo, sharing, testing and "rebuild on the new engine" possible.
  • Ownership. Each thing is either the game's (a:, re-rolled with a new first pass) or yours (u:, placed or pinned, kept). The pin button flips it.
  • Intent is recorded. The auto-decorator records why it placed a thing (hero, forest cluster, shore, near-hero) so the helper can answer "why is that there?" and the taste learner can tell a rule from a roll.
  • Presentation never leaks. The scene file holds world things and settings only; hover, selection and tool state are not saved.

The auto-decorator (first pass) in plain words

  1. Read the land. Slope, height and water for every hex.
  2. Heroes. The family's anchors (barn and house, dome and solar field, tent and wreck) go on the flattest, most central hexes, spaced apart.
  3. Clusters. Trees follow a second noise field so they form woods; fences, haybales and lamps gather near heroes; shore things hug the water.
  4. Scatter. Rocks climb, bushes fill, nothing stands on a slope a building would slide off.
  5. Life. Creatures appear in numbers set by the simulation style and wander only where they can walk.
  6. Polish. The things drop in from the centre outward under the scene's own gravity (on the Moon they float down slowly) with a little dust.

The mock uses hand-written rules like these. The build replaces the placement step with a constraint solver in the wave-function-collapse family (the idea behind Townscaper and many diorama generators), fed with the library's role tags so a "house" can be any of the library's houses and fits its neighbours. The pack allow-list from the project chat (AW-STUDY-0061) decides which models are eligible, and the swipe study's taste learner (AW-STUDY-0060) becomes a ranking prior, so a child's earlier choices tilt the next first pass without a swipe game.

6. The engineering bench

Behind the flask the lab becomes an instrument. The principle: every knob is a registry entry with a name, unit, range, default, level, owner module and a one-line plain explanation. The panels are drawn from the registry, the helper chat is allowed to set only what the registry lists, the scene record stores the values, and developer mode shows the raw table. Adding "fog density" later is one entry, not a new screen.

Bench tabIn the mockIn the build
Land (topology)Relief, feature size, world size, water level, seed, brush size; raise, lower and smooth on the toolbarRivers, erosion pass, terraces, caves and overhangs; stamp shapes (crater, mesa); height import; slope analysis overlay
Sky and weatherTime, real clock, 7 weathers, wind, season; light, sky and particles follow one signalFronts on a seeded chain, tides, fog density, aurora, storms that feed back into crops and creatures; "Always today and now"
Physics and lifeGravity presets and slider, time scale, bounciness, creature count; a drop test where balls fall at your gravity and roll downhill so the land decides where they endRigid bodies via the existing tile-physics, per-prop mass and friction from the model's material roles, wind on trees and cloth, a wake-up budget so big worlds stay smooth
Scene recordEdit log, copy the scene file, rebuild from record with a checksumBranch and compare scenes, restore a step, import a friend's scene, "upgrade" an old scene to the new renderer

Experiments (the part that makes it a lab)

A bench value can be turned into an experiment: choose one or two parameters and a few settings, the lab runs the world forward headless for a number of in-game days (the repo already has ranch-headless.mjs), and shows the outcomes side by side as small diorama cards with a few honest numbers, such as how many creatures thrived, how much grew, how often it stormed. "What if the Moon had rain?" and "What if it was Mars in autumn?" become a tap. Findings can be saved into the scene as notes. This is the same loop as Besiege and Bricktales (build, test, watch, adjust), applied to the world instead of a machine.

7. The helper in the lab (ChatGPT in game)

Evan recently said he does not want the swipe diorama tile game, but does want ChatGPT in the game. The lab is where that fits best: it is a place where plain words really are the fastest tool. The mock's Ask tab understands things like "make it winter", "add 3 trees", "remove the rocks", "moon gravity", "steeper hills", "a storm at night" and "undo", and always says what it did, with an Undo.

  • Same verbs, swappable brain. The helper speaks only registry and edit verbs (move, swap, add, remove, rotate, scale, restyle from the tile-chat contract, plus season, weather, time, gravity, shape). The mock does that with a free pattern matcher. The build sends the same verbs to a model: the AI Gateway today, or ChatGPT as the provider if Evan prefers, behind the wallet caps ($1 a person) and the PG screen. The model returns words for the verbs, never code or asset keys.
  • Everything it does is an edit in the record, so it is undoable, replayable and visible in the Scene tab.
  • The project chat is different. AW-STUDY-0061 passes a request to the project so work gets built. If the helper cannot do something with its verbs (a new kind of tree), it offers "Ask the project to make it", which hands off to that route instead of pretending.
  • Voice later. The helper can speak through an ElevenLabs designed voice; no browser speech, per the invariants.

8. What the Oracle's records say

Fourteen records from the Game Oracle snapshot in the repo informed the shape of the lab. The point is the pattern: the builders children love keep the interface at or under about a tenth of the screen, and the deep simulators that bury you in panels sit at a fifth or more.

GameInterface shareWhat we take
Townscaper4%One palette, the world does the rest. The first pass should feel like this.
Astroneer4%Terrain tool with physical, in-world feedback; the backpack shows its items.
Dorfromantik6%Soft, tactile hex placement; count as the only overlay.
Bad North6%A whole toy island, almost no numbers.
Tiny Glade8%Gridless chemistry: procedural detail around what you draw. A tools tray only.
Besiege8%The thing is the readout. Honest physics, funny failures, build then test.
Minecraft9%A hotbar of blocks is the right shape for the card tray.
LEGO Bricktales, Garry's Mod10%Test run shows success in the world; a spawn menu that grows is the risk.
Cities: Skylines14%Info views that recolour the whole world are a good model for Sky and Land overlays.
Kerbal Space Program18%Precise overlays only where precision pays; it teaches by crashing.
Planet Zoo, RimWorld20% and 22%The depth we want behind the flask but never in front of it.
Spore8%The editor reshapes itself per stage and parts show what they do.

Super Mario Maker and Dreams (design reading in the context card) agree on a second point: creation tools win when the first thing you make is fun in seconds, and when you can play what you made immediately. That is why "Step in" and the running world are in the toolbar, not hidden in a menu.

10. The build plan (six phases, each ends in a passing run)

Sizes are relative effort for one focused thread: S small, M medium, L large. Per the invariants nothing is reachable from abbies.world until it has a real scene and a headless-Chrome run that plays it end to end; until then it lives behind ?exp=scene-builder.

0

Scene document and parameter registry M

Promote this mock's engine into simulations/scene-lab/: aw-scene v1, ops, deterministic fold, checksum, and the parameter registry with units, ranges, levels and owners. Node tests for determinism, undo and migration.

Exit: replay of a 200-edit record is bit-identical; registry covers every parameter in section 4.

1

Recipe to world on real models L

Four choices generate real terrain through the existing terrain code and an auto-decorator over library roles and the pack allow-list. Rendered with the town's three.js and world look. Registry entry scene-builder, experimental.

Exit: headless run picks each family, builds, screenshots six worlds, and checks no engine artifacts (game-feel lint).

2

Free build L

Toolbar, brushes, card tray, bubble, undo and redo, turn, hex glow, placement feel and drop-in with dust, catalogue sounds for every touch (wood, stone, grass), pick and move view, Step in using the existing first-person module.

Exit: a run places, erases, raises, undoes and rebuilds from record; 20 dead-click test passes.

3

The bench L

Land, Sky and weather, Physics and life, Scene record on the registry. Drop test on tile-physics. Experiment runner on the headless sim with side-by-side result cards. Profiler and wake-up budget so a 300-hex world holds frame rate on an iPhone.

Exit: moon versus earth experiment runs headless and the cards agree with a hand calculation; frame-time budget met.

4

Helper and taste M

Extend the tile-chat contract with registry verbs, free matcher first, model behind the wallet and PG screen second, "Ask the project" hand-off, taste prior from votes.

Exit: 30 scripted phrases produce the expected edits; a refused phrase never changes the scene; spend cap test.

5

Door, share and upgrade M

The way in from Winchester, saving a scene as a board or carrying it as an orb, import and export, "upgrade my old worlds" when the renderer improves. Registry flip to live with the end-to-end test; tour decision made with Evan.

Exit: from the town, enter, build, leave, reload and find the world; a v1 scene opens on the newest renderer.

11. Risks and what is deliberately not promised

  • Scope. The bench can swallow the project. Rule: nothing joins the lab without a registry entry, a default, and a test.
  • Performance. Auto-decoration plus physics plus weather on a phone is the real budget. Phase 3 owns it with a profiler, not a hope.
  • Taste of the first pass. Hand-written rules look samey. The solver and the taste prior exist to fix that; phase 1 judges by screenshots shown to Evan.
  • Right-panel drift. A side panel tempts website habits. The card-wall ban applies: facets are slots, lists stay short, the play HUD stays at 8%.
  • Not in this mock: sound (the build uses only catalogue sounds, one per material), real models (stand-in shapes here), real physics engine (a simple fall, bounce and roll here), real AI (pattern matcher here), save to the server.

12. Three calls for Evan

  1. The door. Recommended: the dashed "new world" hex in the board of boards (it already exists in the Changing Worlds study), plus any blank hex. Alternative: a physical workbench in Winchester. Which?
  2. Helper brain. Recommended: the AI Gateway under the wallet caps now, ChatGPT swappable as provider. Or ChatGPT first?
  3. First families. Recommended: Ranch, Woodland and Moon base for phase 1 (richest models), the rest follow. Others first?

Tour: not yet (a study, not reachable from the game). Sounds: none in the mock. Not a minigame story, so no speed review is owed; the numbers to beat are in the phases above.

Try it

Switch to the Lab tab. Press Build my world, pick the Moon family and the crater shape, open the flask, then Drop test. Switch to Earth gravity and drop again. Keys: 1 to 9 cards · Z undo · Q E turn · G hex glow · Space run · F step in · P play · B bench · R new first pass.
